title: How two elections reshaped the India–Bangladesh border

headline: Two elections reshaped India-Bangladesh border

pages.text: A man appeared at the India-Bangladesh border in June 2026. He was 55 years old and had no fingers. People found him in Chapainawabganj. The man said he was an Indian citizen. He told police he had an Aadhaar card.

pages.text: He said Indian authorities pushed him into Bangladesh. He did not cross the border by himself. The police in Bangladesh started a case against him. They used the Control of Entry Act, 1952. The man says he is innocent.

pages.text: This event is part of a bigger problem. Bangladesh and India have a long border. Sometimes, Indian forces push people into Bangladesh. This is called a push-in. It happens often after elections in both countries.

The Border Guard Bangladesh says many people were pushed into their country. They want to use official rules for people moving between countries. However, the two sides often disagree. This makes the border a difficult place for everyone.

A1-A2.headline: Elections Change the India-Bangladesh Border

pages.text: In June 2026, a 55-year-old man named Shreejib Kumar Singh was discovered on the Bangladesh side of the border in Chapainawabganj. Singh, who lacks fingers, claimed he was an Indian citizen from Bihar’s Madhepura district.
pages.caption: Indo-Bangladesh Border in Dakshin Dinajpur, West Bengal, India.

imageProvenance.credit: Indo-Bangladesh Border in Dakshin Dinajpur, West Bengal, India. Image via Wikipedia by Arupparia.

pages.text: He insisted that Indian authorities had wrongly identified him as a Bangladeshi national and forced him across the border. Despite his claims and possession of an Aadhaar card, he was charged under the Control of Entry Act, 1952, by local police. This incident highlights the growing tension along the India-Bangladesh frontier.

imageProvenance.credit: India–Bangladesh Friendship Gate at the Tamabil-Dawki border in northeast Bangladesh. Image via Wikipedia by Ankan.

pages.text: Since the political shifts in 2024 and 2026, the border has become a flashpoint for what authorities call push-ins. This practice involves the informal transfer of individuals across the border without following established legal procedures. Data shows that these attempts have increased significantly, particularly following recent elections in both nations.

The Border Guard Bangladesh has repeatedly urged the Indian Border Security Force to stop these unilateral actions. However, diplomatic talks have struggled to resolve the issue. As both countries navigate new political landscapes, the border remains a site of conflict, leaving individuals like Singh caught in a complex legal and political struggle.

B1-B2.headline: Two elections reshaped India-Bangladesh border

pages.text: The geopolitical landscape of the India–Bangladesh border has undergone a profound transformation, underscored by the recent detention of Shreejib Kumar Singh. In June 2026, Singh, a 55-year-old man with physical disabilities, was apprehended in Chapainawabganj. His testimony contradicts the official narrative; he maintains that he is an Indian citizen from Bihar who was forcibly expelled by Indian authorities.
pages.caption: Indo-Bangladesh Border in Dakshin Dinajpur, West Bengal, India.

imageProvenance.credit: Indo-Bangladesh Border in Dakshin Dinajpur, West Bengal, India. Image via Wikipedia by Arupparia.

pages.text: Despite his assertions and the presentation of an Aadhaar card, he was formally charged under Section 4 of the Control of Entry Act, 1952. This case serves as a microcosm of the broader, contentious practice of cross-border push-ins. The frequency of these extra-legal transfers has escalated following the 2024 political transition in Dhaka and the 2026 West Bengal assembly elections.
pages.caption: India–Bangladesh Friendship Gate in Tamabil-Dawki Border. Image via WIkipedia by Ankan.

imageProvenance.credit: India–Bangladesh Friendship Gate at the Tamabil-Dawki border in northeast Bangladesh. Image via Wikipedia by Ankan.

pages.text: The Bharatiya Janata Party’s electoral success, coupled with its focus on the Citizenship Amendment Act and the revision of electoral rolls, has intensified the pressure on the frontier. Bangladeshi authorities report that thousands have been pushed into their territory, a strategy that persists despite formal protests from the Border Guard Bangladesh. The divergence between the Indian government’s insistence on enforcing domestic law and Bangladesh’s characterization of these actions as a breach of international norms has rendered bilateral cooperation increasingly fragile.

As the border becomes deeply embedded in the electoral calculations of both nations, the human cost remains high. International observers, including Human Rights Watch, have noted the lack of due process in these expulsions. With diplomatic conferences failing to produce substantive changes in ground operations, the border remains a volatile flashpoint, where the lives of individuals are frequently caught in the crossfire of competing national security agendas.

title: How Cambodia’s law on ‘freedom parks’ curtailed people’s right to protest
sourceTitle: How Cambodia’s law on ‘freedom parks’ curtailed people’s right to protest
headline: Cambodia law curtailed right to protest
attribution: Global Voices — original reporting; SAGA AI-assisted educational adaptation
editorialState: Machine screened and source-attributed; not a guarantee of semantic accuracy

pages.text: Cambodia has a law about peaceful protests. It says the government should make freedom parks in every province. These parks are for people to meet and speak. However, the law started in 2009 and only one park exists.

Authorities often stop people from using this space. Groups must tell the government how many people will join a protest. This is hard because no one knows the exact number. If the number is wrong, the protest might be illegal.

The law also does not protect spontaneous protests. These are meetings that happen quickly after an event. Some parks are far from the city. They are near big buildings where no one can see the protesters. This makes it hard for people to share their ideas.

The government also blocks groups from using the main park in Phnom Penh. They use security as a reason to stop them. Human rights groups want to change this law before the elections in 2027 and 2028.

evidence: Cambodia’s Law on Peaceful Demonstration was supposed to ensure the right of citizens to organize and participate in public assemblies by designating freedom parks in every province.
But since its passage in 2009, only one park has been identified, and authorities often impose prohibitions on the use of this space for protests.
As early as 2009, several human rights groups flagged some of the restrictive provisions of the law.
A1-A2.headline: Cambodia Law Limits Public Protests

pages.text: Since 2009, Cambodia’s Law on Peaceful Demonstration has aimed to protect the right to assemble by creating designated freedom parks. However, the implementation has been limited, with only one park identified nationwide. Authorities frequently restrict access to this space, effectively curbing public dissent.

Human rights organizations have long criticized the law’s restrictive nature. A major issue is the requirement for organizers to provide an exact number of participants in advance. Because predicting attendance is impossible, organizers risk having their protests declared illegal if their estimates are inaccurate.

Furthermore, the law fails to recognize spontaneous assemblies, which occur in response to sudden events and cannot be planned in advance. The location of these parks also presents a challenge. In 2017, a new park was established far from the city center, surrounded by industrial buildings, which limits the visibility of protesters.

The government has also used security concerns to block access to the Phnom Penh Freedom Park, notably during the pandemic in 2020. With major elections scheduled for 2027 and 2028, activists are calling for a review of the law to ensure that democratic space is preserved for all citizens.

evidence: The notification letter of the organizers of the planned demonstration will have to include a number of elements, including the number of participants involved in the demonstration.
This requirement is absurd, since it is impossible to predict, ahead of a protest, how many people will join.
If the estimates of the organizers appear to be inaccurate, under a strict interpretation of the law, the protest could be considered illegal.
B1-B2.headline: Cambodia law curtailed right to protest

pages.text: The Cambodian Law on Peaceful Demonstration, enacted in 2009, was ostensibly designed to facilitate public assembly by mandating the designation of freedom parks in every province. In practice, however, the legislation has served as a mechanism for state control. Only a single park has been officially identified, and authorities frequently invoke security concerns to prohibit its use, thereby undermining the very rights the law was intended to safeguard.

Legal experts and human rights groups have identified several structural flaws. The mandatory notification process requires organizers to estimate participant numbers—a logistical impossibility that renders protests vulnerable to being declared illegal based on inaccurate projections. Moreover, the law is notably silent regarding spontaneous assemblies, which are essential for responding to immediate socio-political developments. This lack of legal recognition effectively criminalizes unplanned public expression.

Geographic marginalization further exacerbates these restrictions. The 2017 relocation of the Phnom Penh Freedom Park to an isolated industrial zone significantly diminished the expressive value of demonstrations by removing them from the public eye. Documented instances, such as the 2015 blocking of eviction-hit communities and the 2020 installation of barricades, illustrate a pattern of state interference.

As Cambodia approaches the 2027 and 2028 election cycles, civil society organizations are intensifying their calls for legislative reform, arguing that the current application of the law reduces democracy to a mere electoral exercise, stifling the agency of citizens in the public sphere.

evidence: A related concern is the lack of recognition and protection in the [law] for spontaneous assemblies.
Spontaneous assemblies are those that occur without prior organization, usually in response to a specific event.
Because they are unplanned, prior notification is not possible.
